title: DICE: Decoupling Capability from Intervention Necessity in LLM Tutoring
claim: Existing tutors fail by over-intervening on correct answers or accepting wrong ones; explicit action selection intervenes only when needed.
layout: 2 scenario panels, each with existing-vs-ours dialogue cards, read top-down, color-coded
description: Two side-by-side scenarios, each with a colored header banner. Scenario A (orange) is over-intervention: the student answers correctly. Scenario B (red) is false acceptance: the student answers incorrectly. Below each header is a gray question card with a pinned answer tag (6 homs/$24 and 620). Beneath that are two dog-eared paper-style dialogue cards. The left card, 'Existing tutors', is tinted orange or red. The right card, 'DICE', is tinted light blue with a blue border. Each card holds turn-by-turn Student/Teacher transcripts. Green and red text highlights correct and erroneous teacher feedback. Italic notes mark skipped turns, such as 'continues intervention for 5 more turns'. The eye goes first to the colored banners, then to the contrast between the left and right dialogue cards.
caption: Two failure modes of existing tutors (SocraticLM used for this case) and how DICE addresses them through explicit action selection. Scenario A: The student solves the problem correctly, but SocraticLM continues guiding for three unnecessary turns before confirming. Scenario B: the student produces an arithmetic error, but SocraticLM accepts the wrong answer; DICE redirects the student to the faulty step. Full dialogue rollouts are in Appendix [ref].
abstract: Fluent guidance is not the same as useful intervention. LLM tutors are typically trained to generate the next teacher utterance, implicitly assuming that every student turn warrants a response. However, our experiments indicate that this conflates tutoring capability (what to say) with intervention necessity (whether to say it). We introduce DICE, a framework that decouples intervention decisions from response generation by first selecting an explicit pedagogical action. To calibrate this action selection policy, we define Intervention Value (IV), a rollout-grounded counterfactual metric that compares each action against non-intervention. IV shows that many prescribed interventions provide little or no marginal benefit. We further introduce DICE-Bench, a multi-variant math tutoring benchmark with skill-preserving problem variants for session-level evaluation. Using IV-weighted and KL-regularized policy optimization, DICE learns to intervene selectively while preserving tutoring effectiveness. In simulated tutoring sessions, DICE reduces the over-intervention rate to near zero while guiding students to correct solutions in approximately 3-4 fewer turns on average than existing Socratic tutoring baselines.
